column1: # The ruling sheet of the cross-connection trial (docs/UPPER.md §17, question 52).
# These edges hold in Claude's everyday reading, and no source says them: not Wikidata's subclass
# statements, not WordNet's tree, not the WordNet gloss (align/trial-cross-animal.tsv).
# ruling: Peter ruled them all by one rule on 2026-11-12: a pack is strict, an edge with a
#   counterexample stays out, and whoever wants it adds it to a store of their own. Claude applied
#   the rule: no where a kind is known, or held on good grounds, to fall outside the class (the
#   kind follows the no), yes where none is known. Peter may change any ruling here: yes or no, and
#   after it any remark; an empty cell makes the edge wait. A row added for any other candidate of
#   the table is read too, so a yes puts back an edge the strict reading left out. A yes is also a
#   yes to every class above the one named (UPPER.md §16: an edge is wrong if an ancestor it brings
#   in is false of the child); the classes above are named on each class's line below.
#   tools/cross_trial.py reads this column: it applies an edge ruled yes and leaves out one ruled no.
# note: what the reading rests on, and what else is worth knowing.
n
column5: note

column1: # --- aquatic-animal: an animal that lives in water ---

column5: Every jellyfish lives in water: most kinds in the sea, a few in lakes and rivers, which is why marine-animal was read as false of it. Gloss: usually marine and free-swimming.
Sea prawns and freshwater prawns alike. Follows from prawn ⊑ shellfish as well.
Sea clams and freshwater clams alike. Follows from clam ⊑ shellfish, which Wikidata states, so it holds whatever the ruling; it is here because the trial has it as a row.

column1: # --- marine-animal: an animal that lives in the sea; above it: aquatic-animal ---

column4: no: a few kinds of its family live in brackish lagoons and in the Caspian
column5: WordNet's cockle is the common European one, of sandy shores and river mouths. Without this edge the cockle is still under aquatic-animal, by shellfish.
No octopus lives in fresh water.
No squid lives in fresh water; one small kind comes into bays and river mouths, which are still the sea.
Every echinoderm lives in the sea, none in fresh water or on land.
As the sea cucumber. The gloss says shallow-water, which stops short of the sea.

column1: # --- shellfish: an aquatic mollusc or crustacean with a shell; above it: aquatic-animal, invertebrate ---
# WordNet's own shellfish is another word for mollusk, and its other sense is the meat; neither is this class.

column4: no: land crabs live out of water
column5: The crabs people eat are of the sea and of rivers; a yes would put every crab under aquatic-animal.
A crustacean of the sea. Gloss: edible marine crustaceans.
A crustacean of the sea and of fresh water.
A sea snail. Gloss: large edible marine gastropods having an ear-shaped shell.
Gloss: common edible, burrowing European bivalve mollusk that has a strong, rounded shell. Every cockle lives in water.
Gloss: marine or freshwater bivalve mollusk.
Gloss: edible marine bivalve having a fluted fan-shaped shell.

column1: # --- flying-animal: an animal that can fly (read of the grown animal, not of the chick or the caterpillar) ---

column5: Every kind of bat flies. The gloss stops at forelimbs modified to form membranous wings.
Every living kind of owl flies.
Every living kind of pigeon and dove flies. The dodo, of the same family, did not; nobody calls it a pigeon.

column4: no: three of the four kinds of steamer duck and two island teals of New Zealand cannot fly
column5: Most ducks fly.
Every kind of bee flies.
Every kind of butterfly flies.
Every kind of mosquito flies.

column1: # --- carnivore: an animal that eats mainly other animals ---

column5: No snake eats plants; even the egg-eating snakes live on animal food.

column4: no: tadpoles graze on algae, and one Brazilian tree frog eats fruit
column5: Grown frogs eat insects and other small animals.
Seals eat fish, squid and krill, and the leopard seal penguins. Follows from seal ⊑ predator as well.
Toothed whales and dolphins (dolphin is below whale here) eat fish and squid; baleen whales eat krill and small fish, which are animals.

column1: # --- herbivore: an animal that eats mainly plants ---

column5: Eats grass, leaves, bark and fruit. Wikidata gives its main food source as plant.
Eats grass and other plants.
Eats grass, herbs and bark.
Eats desert plants. The gloss calls it cud-chewing, and the cud is plants.
Grazes and browses. The node took over WordNet's ass under the name donkey (rulings-v14-ysenses.tsv); the wild asses it covers graze too.
The offspring of a donkey and a horse, and fed as they are.
Eats grass, hay and vegetables. The node is the pet rodent since the everyday-sense pass (rulings-v14-ysenses.tsv).
Grazes on seaweed and algae.

column1: # --- predator: an animal that lives by preying on other animals; above it: carnivore ---

column5: Hunts deer, wild pig and other large animals. Wikidata gives its food as ungulates, monkeys, fish, rabbits and hares. WordNet's tree states tiger ⊑ carnivore already.
House cats and wildcats hunt (WordNet's cat covers both). Wikidata lists predation among the house cat's characteristics. WordNet's tree states cat ⊑ carnivore already.

column4: no: the egg-eating snakes of Africa and India live on birds' eggs alone
column5: Other snakes take live prey. Without this edge the snake is still under carnivore, by its own row.
Hunts crabs, shellfish and fish. Wikidata gives its food as fish, scallops, snails, worms and small crustaceans.
Hunts fish and shrimp. Wikidata gives its food as fish, arrow worms, krill and zooplankton.
Hunts fish and squid.
Hunts fish, squid and krill; the leopard seal takes penguins and other seals.

column4: no: the upside-down jellyfish lives mostly on the algae in its tissue
column5: Most jellyfish catch small animals with their stinging tentacles. Wikidata gives the food as fish, fish larvae, roe and plankton.
Hunts earthworms and grubs underground.

column4: no: tadpoles graze on algae, and one Brazilian tree frog eats fruit
column5: Grown frogs catch insects, worms and smaller animals alive.
A tuna; hunts small fish, squid and crustaceans in schools.
The tunas of the genus Thunnus hunt fish and squid.

column1: # --- domestic-animal: an animal of a kind people have domesticated ---

column5: The donkey is the domesticated form of the African wild ass. The node took over WordNet's ass, which covers the wild asses too; the name donkey, read in its everyday sense, does not.

column4: no: the wild Bactrian camel of the Gobi is a kind of its own that never was domesticated
column5: The dromedary and the Bactrian camel are domesticated.

column1: # --- venomous-animal: an animal that injects venom ---

column5: Every jellyfish has stinging cells that inject venom, though the sting of many kinds does not get through human skin.
